sections.text: A trait describes something a type can do. It lists method signatures, and any type can promise to provide them. You have already met one: Display is the trait for "can be shown with {}". Now you will write your own.

trait Speak { ... } defines the trait. Inside, a method signature ending in a semicolon is required: every type that wants the trait must write its own body. A method with a body is a default method: types get it for free, and may override it. impl Speak for Dog gives a type the trait.

Dog only wrote name and sound, and got intro for free. Robot wrote its own intro, which replaces the default. Inside a trait, self.name() calls another method of the same trait; this works for every type that implements it. Dog and Robot are unrelated types, but both can Speak.

This is the same shape as the impl fmt::Display for LoginError you saw, and the one for ShopError you wrote, in Unit 6. Display is a trait from the standard library. It asks for one method, fmt, and the {} in println! calls it. Here it is again for a new type:
Once a type implements Display, Rust also gives it a to_string method for free. That is the power of traits: implement one small thing and get more.
A trait is a promise. impl Speak for Dog is a signed promise that Dog has every method Speak lists. If you forget a required method, the compiler tells you which one.

Traits are like interfaces in Java, C# and Go, with default methods. Unlike Go, a type must say impl Trait for Type explicitly. Unlike Java, you can implement your own trait for a type from someone else's crate, such as i32 or String. The orphan rule keeps this safe: you may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. That is why you can't implement Display for Vec<i32> yourself.

exercise.prompt: The starter has a Speak trait with a required speak method and a default shout method. Dog already implements it. Make Robot speak too: its speak should return beep followed by a space and its id. Then, at the end of main, create a Robot with id 7 and print its shout. It should print two lines: WOOF, I AM REX and BEEP 7. The compiler warns that Robot is never constructed until you finish; that is expected. Hint: impl Speak for Robot { fn speak(&self) -> String { format!("beep {}", self.id) } }

quiz.question: In a trait, what is a default method?
options: A method with a body in the trait, which types get for free and may replace
A method that Rust calls automatically when a value of the type is created
A method with no body, which every type must write for itself

quiz.question: Which line gives the type Robot the trait Speak?
After you implement Display for a type, what else can you do with it?
options: Print it with {:?} and compare two values with ==
Print it with {} and call to_string on it
Copy it instead of moving it, and print it with {:?}
